title: Why Nations Fail: The Origins of Power, Prosperity, and Poverty

contents: Nogales, halved: one city, two nations, and the whole question in a fence
Theories that don't work: geography, culture, and the ignorance of leaders each rejected
Extractive versus inclusive institutions, economic and political, and how each pair locks together
Critical junctures and small differences: the Black Death, the Glorious Revolution, and why England industrialised first
The iron law of oligarchy and the vicious circle of extraction
Creative destruction and why extractive elites block the technologies that would enrich their nations
Growth under extraction — the Soviet Union and China — and why the book predicts it cannot last
Virtuous circles: how inclusive institutions defend and deepen themselves

audiences: Readers of Guns, Germs, and Steel wanting the institutions rebuttal
Anyone asking why some nations are rich and others poor now
Students of political economy and development
Policy readers weighing aid, growth, and democratisation

sources.title: Why Nations Fail
sources.supports: Publication facts (Crown Business, 2012-03-20, 546pp, ISBN 0307719219), the inclusive/extractive thesis, the Nogales opening, the rejected rival hypotheses, and the documented reception on both sides including the named critiques.

sources.title: What Makes Countries Rich or Poor? (as documented in the book's reception record)
sources.author_or_publisher: Jared Diamond, The New York Review of Books
sources.supports: The geography camp's documented rebuttal-in-kind: institutions matter but the book dismisses geographic factors too completely, and its critical-juncture history undersells broader patterns — the mirror image of the authors' critique of Diamond.
sources.limitations: Accessed via documented summary; Diamond is the opposing theorist reviewing his rivals.

sources.title: Good Ideas, But Missing Analysis (as documented in the reception record)
sources.supports: The most famous negative verdict: the inclusive/extractive dichotomy applied too vaguely and the book overall 'a major disappointment'.
sources.limitations: Accessed via documented quotation; a philanthropist-technologist's review, not an economist's.

sources.title: Government, Geography, and Growth (as documented in the reception record)
sources.supports: A development economist's documented critique: the theory focuses too narrowly on domestic institutions, ignoring technology and geopolitics, and authoritarian Asian growth does not fit.
sources.limitations: Accessed via documented summary; Sachs is a rival theorist.

sources.title: The circularity objection (as documented in the reception record)
sources.supports: The methodological objection: institutions are inferred good where outcomes are good, and modernisation may cause institutions rather than the reverse — with China as the standing counterexample the authors answer by prediction.

sources.title: The Sveriges Riksbank Prize in Economic Sciences 2024
sources.supports: The 2024 prize to Acemoglu, Johnson, and Robinson 'for studies of how institutions are formed and affect prosperity' — the research programme behind the book, honoured at the discipline's highest level.
sources.limitations: Honours the underlying research, not the popular book as such.

sources.title: Review of Why Nations Fail (as documented in the reception record)
sources.supports: The praise side's documented register: 'bracing, garrulous, wildly ambitious... may be a bit of a masterpiece'.

sources.title: Why Nations Fail
sources.supports: A decade of warm-but-argumentative reader reception: praised as the institutions primer, with recurring complaints about repetition and the same-example-again structure.

workflow.coverage_notes: Built from the documented record, the named specialist critiques on both sides of the geography-institutions debate, the Nobel documentation of the underlying research, and reader reception.
